Variants.Content: Bologna's studium, its university of law, drew students from across Europe and claimed to be the oldest continuously operating university in the West. Its scholars revived the study of Roman law through the Corpus Juris Civilis, and masters called glossators, Accursius among them, set the texts into commentaries that shaped legal teaching for centuries. The city itself was a Guelph commune, governed by its own councils and largely independent of imperial lordship in daily affairs. Patrician families raised soaring brick towers, including the twin Asinelli and Garisenda, and rival clans turned the streets into a battlefield whenever a feud flared. Academic prestige and urban warfare shared the same walls, and the commune depended on both to keep its voice in Italian politics.
Self-governing student nation guilds held civic magistrates accountable, turning the commune into an unassailable bastion of legal jurisprudence.
